summary:
Nehemiah continues Ezra (the two were a single book in Hebrew tradition), mostly as first-person memoir. Nehemiah is cupbearer to King Artaxerxes — the official who served the king's wine — in the Persian citadel of Susa when word arrives that the survivors of the exile (the deportation to Babylon in 586 BC) are "in great trouble and disgrace": Jerusalem's wall is broken down, its gates burned (1:3). It is 445 BC, some ninety years after the first exiles returned. Nehemiah fasts and prays, then asks the king for leave, letters of safe passage, and timber. In Jerusalem he inspects the ruined wall by night before telling anyone why he has come, then puts it to the leaders: "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, so that we will no longer be a disgrace" (2:17).

Chapters 3–6 build the wall under pressure from Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem — leaders in the neighboring provinces — who move from mockery to armed threats to invitations Nehemiah takes for traps. He arms the workforce — the laborers "worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other" (4:17) — and answers repeated summonses with "I am doing a great work and cannot come down" (6:3). He also stops nobles from seizing the fields and children of indebted fellow Jews (chapter 5). The wall "was completed in fifty-two days" (6:15); even the surrounding nations "realized that this task had been accomplished by our God" (6:16).

The book then turns to the community inside the wall. Ezra the scribe reads the Law aloud at the Water Gate "from daybreak until noon" while Levites (the tribe set apart to assist in the temple) move through the crowd "explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read" (8:3, 8). The listeners weep and are told to feast instead: "the joy of the LORD is your strength" (8:10). They keep the Feast of Booths — a week in leafy shelters, recalling the wilderness years — confess the nation's history in a long prayer (chapter 9), and sign a pledge on tithes (the tenth of produce owed for the temple staff), the Sabbath, and intermarriage: "we will not neglect the house of our God" (10:39). Chapter 13 tests the pledge: back in Persia for a time, Nehemiah returns to find Tobiah lodged in a temple storeroom, the Levites and singers "gone back to their own fields" unpaid, Sabbath trading at the gates, and new foreign marriages; he throws Tobiah's furniture out, restores the tithes, and shuts the city gates for the Sabbath. Withheld tithes and foreign marriages are the complaints the prophet Malachi also presses (Malachi 3:8–10; 2:11), one reason Malachi is often dated to this generation. The book's last words are Nehemiah's refrain: "Remember me, O my God, with favor" (13:31).
